title: ONAN’S SIN WAS BIGGER THAN THE PHYSICAL ACT EVERYONE FIXATES ON
paragraphs: ONAN’S SIN WAS BIGGER THAN THE PHYSICAL ACT EVERYONE FIXATES ON
Everyone remembers what Onan did with his body. Almost nobody slows down long enough to ask what was happening in his heart.
And that changes the way you read the entire story.

Because Genesis 38 is not merely preserving an ancient account about a sexual act. It is exposing something frighteningly familiar: the human ability to receive the benefits of a relationship while deliberately refusing the responsibility that comes with it.
That is where this story gets uncomfortably close to us.
Onan wanted something from Tamar.
He simply did not want to give Tamar what his responsibility required.
And somewhere between those two realities, Scripture gives us one of the Bible’s shortest and most sobering portraits of calculated selfishness.
The story begins in a broken household.

Judah’s firstborn son, Er, married a woman named Tamar. Scripture tells us that Er was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD put him to death. We are not told precisely what Er did. The Bible refuses to satisfy our curiosity.
Then Judah turned to his second son, Onan.
Genesis 38:8 records Judah telling him to fulfill his responsibility toward his deceased brother’s wife and raise offspring for his brother.
The Hebrew becomes especially important here.
וְיַבֵּם אֹתָהּ
wəyabbēm ʾōtāh
The key verb is יָבַם — yābam.
It refers to performing the duty of a brother-in-law toward the widow of a deceased brother.
Judah continues:
וְהָקֵם זֶרַע לְאָחִיךָ
wəhāqēm zeraʿ ləʾāḥîkā
“Raise up offspring for your brother.”
The word זֶרַע — zeraʿ — can mean seed, offspring, or descendants depending on context.
This matters enormously.
The passage itself tells us what Onan understood.
Genesis 38:9 says:
וַיֵּדַע אוֹנָן כִּי לֹּא לוֹ יִהְיֶה הַזָּרַע
Wayyēdaʿ ʾÔnān kî lō lô yihyeh hazzāraʿ.
“And Onan knew that the offspring would not be his.”
There it is.
The narrator takes us inside his reasoning.
Onan knew.
That may be the most terrifying phrase in the story.
He was not confused.
He was not ignorant of what was expected.
He knew.

And because he knew that the resulting offspring would be reckoned to his dead brother rather than to himself, Genesis tells us that whenever he went in to Tamar, he deliberately prevented conception.
Read that carefully.
He did not simply refuse the arrangement openly.
He participated in the part that benefited him while sabotaging the part that benefited someone else.
That is why reducing the entire account to one isolated physical action can cause us to miss a major emphasis of the narrator.
The text explicitly gives Onan’s motive.
He knew the offspring would not be his, and therefore he acted “so that he would not give offspring to his brother.”
That final purpose clause matters.
His body was carrying out a decision his heart had already made.

This does not mean Christians throughout history have agreed on every moral question people later associated with this passage. They have not. Different Christian traditions have drawn different conclusions concerning sexual ethics and contraception from Genesis 38.
We should be careful not to force the passage to answer every later debate by itself.
But we should be equally careful not to erase what Genesis explicitly says.
Onan knowingly took what he wanted while deliberately withholding what he owed.
He treated Tamar as though her body could serve his desires while her future could remain somebody else’s problem.
And suddenly this ancient story does not feel ancient anymore.
Because Onan’s pattern did not die with Onan.
We can do the same thing without ever standing anywhere near Genesis 38.
We want the comfort of marriage without sacrificial love.
The benefits of church without serving anyone.
The promises of God without surrender to God.
Forgiveness without repentance.
Christian community without accountability.
A platform without responsibility.
Influence without integrity.
Grace without transformation.
We want Jesus as Savior while quietly negotiating whether He may also be Lord.
Take what benefits me.
Withhold what costs me.
That is the heartbeat beneath so much human rebellion.
And God sees it.
Genesis 38:10 says that what Onan did was evil “in the eyes of the LORD.”
The Hebrew reads:
וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה
Wayyēraʿ bəʿênê YHWH ʾăšer ʿāśāh.
“What he did was evil in the eyes of YHWH.”
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not merely tell us that ancient society disapproved.
It does not say Judah found it embarrassing.
It does not say Tamar complained.
The narrator takes us directly into the courtroom that ultimately matters.
The eyes of the LORD.
People saw an ordinary family arrangement.
God saw the heart behind it.
People could see Onan entering Tamar’s life.
God could see why.
And there are few truths more comforting—or more terrifying—than this:
God sees motives that human beings cannot.
You can look obedient while resisting God internally.
You can stand in church with your hands raised while keeping entire rooms of your life locked.
You can know the worship songs.
Know the Bible verses.
Know Christian language.
Know exactly when to say “Amen.”
And still quietly tell Jesus:
“You can have everything except this.”
Maybe that is why Onan’s story makes us uncomfortable when we stop arguing about the physical mechanics long enough to listen.
Because suddenly Onan is not merely “that man in Genesis.”
Suddenly the question becomes:
What am I withholding from God because obedience would cost me something?
That question reaches deeper than sexual ethics.
Maybe you know you need to forgive someone, but resentment feels too valuable to surrender.
Maybe you know you need to confess something, but your reputation feels too valuable to risk.
Maybe there is a relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ, but loneliness terrifies you.
Maybe money has quietly become your security.
Maybe pornography has become your hidden refuge.
Maybe pride has made apology almost impossible.
Maybe you serve publicly while starving spiritually.
Maybe you keep asking God to bless a life you have never fully surrendered to Him.
And perhaps nobody knows.
That is the frightening part.
Nobody knew everything happening inside Onan either.
But God did.
The Gospel never gives us permission to hide behind outward appearances.
Jesus repeatedly confronted precisely that kind of religion.

People could clean the outside while corruption remained within. People could honor God with their lips while their hearts remained far from Him. People could appear righteous before others while God saw beneath the performance.
Christ has never been interested merely in managing appearances.
He came for the heart.
And this is where Genesis 38 becomes even more astonishing.
Because if the chapter ended with judgment, it would already be sobering.
But Genesis does not end there.
The story keeps moving.
Judah fails Tamar too.
Tamar eventually takes desperate and morally complicated action.
Judah is exposed.
A pregnancy follows.
Twins are born.
One of them is Perez.
And generations later, another genealogy appears.
Matthew begins telling the story of Jesus Christ.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Judah.
And then Matthew does something remarkable.
He names Tamar.
“Judah fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar.”
The scandal was not erased from the family history of the Messiah.
God put it in the genealogy.
Not because sin does not matter.
Genesis 38 makes painfully clear that it does.
But because human failure cannot prevent God from accomplishing His redemptive purpose.
Perez enters the line that eventually leads to David.
And through David’s royal line, according to the flesh, comes Jesus Christ.
Think about that.
A chapter containing death, selfishness, sexual brokenness, deception, exploitation, shame, family dysfunction, and public exposure becomes part of the road toward Bethlehem.
Only God writes stories like that.
We would have edited Genesis 38 out.
God preserved it.
We would have hidden Tamar.
Matthew named her.
We would have cleaned up the Messiah’s genealogy before publishing it.
God displayed the broken family tree and then placed Jesus at its culmination.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that respectable people managed to produce a Savior.
Christianity is the announcement that a Savior entered the wreckage of humanity to rescue sinners.
That Savior is Jesus.
He did what Onan would not.
Onan acted according to what served himself.
Christ came not to be served, but to serve and to give His life as a ransom for many.
Onan withheld what would cost him.
Jesus withheld nothing necessary for our redemption.
Onan’s story exposes the instinct to protect ourselves at another person’s expense.
Jesus willingly gave Himself for people who had nothing with which to repay Him.
At Calvary, Christ did not exploit the vulnerable.
He became vulnerable.
He was mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Pierced.
Crucified.
And He remained obedient to the Father even unto death.
There is the contrast our hearts desperately need.
Not merely Onan versus better behavior.
Onan versus Christ.
Self-protection versus self-giving love.
Calculated selfishness versus holy obedience.
Taking versus giving.
Sin versus righteousness.
Death versus resurrection.
And here is where the Gospel becomes personal.
You do not overcome the Onan inside the human heart merely by trying harder.
Sin runs deeper than behavior.
Jesus said evil proceeds from within the human heart.
We need more than external restraint.
We need a new heart.
That is why Christ did not come merely to make immoral people more respectable.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
He bore sin on the cross.
He rose from the dead.
He calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
And repentance is not God humiliating you for finally admitting what He already knows.
Repentance is dropping the disguise.
It is coming into the light.
It is saying:
“Jesus, I have taken what I wanted and withheld what You asked.”
“I have used people.”
“I have protected my idols.”
“I have excused what I should have confessed.”
“I have looked obedient while negotiating with You privately.”
“I have sinned.”
And then grace does what shame never could.
Grace does not tell you the sin was harmless.
Grace tells you the blood of Christ is sufficient.
Grace does not rename darkness as light.
Grace brings you out of darkness.
Grace does not say, “Stay exactly as you are.”
Grace says, “Come to Jesus exactly as you are—and He will not leave you exactly as you are.”
This is why our message has always been:
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
He does something greater.
He redeems sinners.
Peter still denied Him.
Paul still persecuted Christians.
The woman at the well still had her history.
The thief still reached the cross guilty.
Tamar’s name still appears in a complicated story.
Judah’s failure is still written in Genesis.
Yet failure did not receive the final word.
Jesus did.
And maybe you needed that tonight.
Maybe you have been reading this thinking about someone else.
Someone selfish.
Someone sexually broken.
Someone hypocritical.
Someone who hurt you.
Someone who used you.
But perhaps somewhere along the way the Holy Spirit turned the mirror around.
And now you are thinking about you.
Do not run from that moment.
Run to Christ.
There is no freedom in defending the darkness Jesus came to forgive.
Confess it.
Bring it into the light.
Repent.
Believe.
Ask for help.
Seek accountability where needed.
If you have sinned against someone, pursue biblical reconciliation where it is safe and appropriate.
If a hidden habit has mastered you, stop protecting it.
If you have been performing Christianity while starving inside, tell Jesus the truth.
He already knows.
The wonder of the Gospel is that the One who knows you most completely is the One whose grace is sufficient for every sinner who comes to Him in faith.
So be honest.
Did this hit harder than you expected?
If God exposed something you have been hiding, you can comment, “Jesus forgive me.”
If you are exhausted but refuse to walk away from Christ, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray with you, simply comment, “pray for me.”
And if you are watching Jesus patiently rebuild areas of your life you once thought were beyond redemption, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Sometimes somebody scrolling through those comments needs to discover that they are not the only Christian fighting a battle behind a smile.
Your honesty may become someone else’s invitation into the light.
And if one person came to mind while reading this, do not merely think about them.
Send it privately to the believer who has grown cold.
Share it with the person who thinks their past has permanently disqualified them from grace.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ.
Come to Jesus.
Not to a brand.
Not to a personality.
Not to merchandise.
Not to religious performance.
Jesus.
The One who knows what you did.
The One who knows why you did it.
The One who sees the secret compromises nobody else sees.
The One who calls sin what it is.
And the One who went to the cross so sinners could be forgiven, cleansed, reconciled to God, and transformed.
Onan’s tragedy was bigger than the physical act everyone remembers.
His outward action revealed an inward refusal.
And perhaps that is the warning Genesis 38 still whispers across thousands of years:
God is not merely watching what our hands do.
He sees what our hearts refuse to surrender.
So do not give Jesus the appearance of obedience while secretly reserving the throne for yourself.
Give Him the hidden room.
Give Him the wound.
Give Him the appetite.
Give Him the resentment.
Give Him the relationship.
Give Him the shame.
Give Him the secret.
Give Him the future.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive the mercy purchased at the cross.
Then rise and walk differently—not because your obedience purchases grace, but because grace has found you.
And remember this when your past starts whispering that God could never make anything beautiful from what happened:
There was scandal in the family tree that led to Bethlehem, but scandal did not get the final word.
Jesus did.
And He still does.
